raw_case_text:
A 74-year-old male was admitted to the emergency department due to sudden aphasia, left facial palsy, and difficulty swallowing. Both his sister and son were diagnosed with epilepsy, presumably due to neurocysticercosis.
He was diagnosed with structural epilepsy suspected to be secondary to intraparenchymal neurocysticercosis and received a single course of albendazole. The patient had been on carbamazepine 200 mg bid for most of his life, with regular seizure control reporting a frequency of one seizure a year.
Upon examination, he had disseminated skin lesions located in the upper thorax, abdomen, and all limbs and mucous membranes. The lesions consisted of violet and skin-colored nodules and macules, ranging from 0.5 mm to 2 cm. Nodular neoformations were rubbery, adherent, and seemed to be vascular in nature; skin biopsies were taken (Figures 1A,B).
On neurological examination, the patient had bilateral abducens nerve palsy, left central facial palsy, and left soft-palate palsy, accompanied by a diminished ipsilateral gag reflex. His tongue deviated to the left upon protrusion and he had a discrete left-body weakness with ipsilateral extensor plantar response. He exhibited left-side dysmetria on finger-to-nose test.
A brain computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a large, right frontal hematoma in acute and subacute phases with perilesional edema and no deviation of the mid-line structures, multiple calcified intraparenchymal lesions, as well as a punctiform hemorrhage within the medulla oblongata (Figure 1C). A computed tomography angiography (AngioCT) of the head was performed, confirming multiple heterogeneous contrast-enhancing vascular malformations in the cortical and subcortical areas of both cerebral hemispheres. Brain MRI showed in FLAIR a moderately differentiated hyperintense lesion located in the right frontotemporal region, with irregular borders, measuring 26.7 x 37.7 mm in its largest dimension, with abundant perilesional edema and an irregular core, as well as two lesions located in the right occipital lobe measuring almost 10 mm in diameter each, and another hypointense lesion measuring 10.5 mm in its largest diameter in the left temporal pole. On T2* gradient-echo (GRE), numerous supra and infratentorial punctate hypointense foci were observed. Infratentorial lesions included multiple hypointense lesions in the cerebellum, both in the vermis, and each hemisphere, a hypointense pontine lesion with a diameter of 10.5 mm, and a lesion in the midbrain that measured 6 x 5 mm. This pattern was consistent with CCM:like lesions (Figures 2C,D).
The following week, the patient presented with respiratory distress. A thorax CT was performed, which showed multilobar pneumonia. Intravenous, wide-spectrum antibiotics were initiated, and Staphylococcus aureus was isolated from the blood and sputum samples. He died in the next few days, and an autopsy was performed.
Histopathology of the brain tissue revealed multiple arteriovenous malformations characterized by poorly formed vessels with incomplete walls and a deposit of hyaline material, surrounded by abundant collagen and with areas of cerebral parenchyma, macrophages with hemosiderin, and vascular ectasia. These malformations had different sizes and locations; some were calcified. Additionally, there was intraparenchymal hemorrhage at the basal ganglia (Figures 2A,B).
Dermatologic histopathology reported skin lesions with multiple vascular proliferations with areas of dilated and congestive venous vessels, ectasia, and extensively hyalinized, focal, or complete disassembly of the middle tunic. A separation into inner or outer layers by an aberrant elastic lamina was also observed (Figure 1D). Based on these findings, the diagnosis of blue nevus syndrome was made.
Because this syndrome may present as an autosomal dominant inheritance, an extensive examination of the patient's relatives was performed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 74-year-old man presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset aphasia, left facial palsy, and dysphagia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was admitted to the emergency department following the abrupt onset of aphasia, left-sided facial weakness, and difficulty swallowing. One week into hospitalization, he developed acute respiratory distress.
subjective.past_medical_history: Longstanding history of structural epilepsy (~1 seizure per year controlled on carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily) previously attributed to intraparenchymal neurocysticercosis and treated with a single course of albendazole. Family history was notable for epilepsy in both his sister and his son, also previously presumed secondary to neurocysticercosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Taking carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily prior to admission.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatological examination revealed disseminated 0.5 mm to 2 cm violet and skin-colored rubbery, adherent vascular nodules and macules over the upper thorax, abdomen, all four extremities, and oral mucous membranes. Neurological examination showed aphasia, bilateral abducens nerve (CN VI) palsies, left central facial palsy, left soft-palate palsy with diminished ipsilateral gag reflex, leftward tongue deviation on protrusion, mild left hemiparesis with a left extensor plantar response, and left-sided dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing.
objective.routine_investigations: During his second hospital week, blood and sputum cultures isolated Staphylococcus aureus.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT, head CTA, and brain MRI (including FLAIR and T2* gradient-echo sequences) revealed a large acute/subacute right frontotemporal intraparenchymal hematoma (26.7 x 37.7 mm) with perilesional edema, multiple calcified parenchymal lesions, a punctiform hemorrhage in the medulla oblongata, and numerous supra- and infratentorial heterogeneous contrast-enhancing cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM)-like vascular lesions (right occipital lobe, left temporal pole, cerebellar vermis/hemispheres, pons, and midbrain). Chest CT during week 2 showed multilobar pneumonia.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Despite broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics for multilobar Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia and bacteremia, the patient died and underwent autopsy. Brain and skin histopathology revealed multiple cerebral vascular/arteriovenous malformations with hyalinized incomplete vessel walls, calcifications, hemosiderin-laden macrophages, and basal ganglia hemorrhage alongside cutaneous venous malformations with aberrant elastic laminae, establishing a definitive diagnosis of autosomal dominant blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome (previously misdiagnosed in the patient and his family as calcified neurocysticercosis).
